metadata.title: What It Had to Guess
metadata.audience: A hiring manager or engineer deciding whether the author can tell a verified claim from an unverified one
metadata.greeting_note: The assignment requires narrating as myself and forbids the instructor's name, persona or credit line, so the toolkit's claude-liam persona, IN-FOR-BEAR LAW and the @NikBearBrown outro lock are deliberately not used. The voice is synthetic and B00 says so in its first breath.
metadata.source: Pepper — The Personal AI Prompter, v0.3 (pepper-v0.3.zip): CHANGES.md, pepper-extension/README.md, PRIVACY.md, manifest.json, lib/core.js, pepper-tests/README.md, docs/LIVE-TEST-PROTOCOL.md. Alternatives read on their own pages, 10 Oct 2026: help.openai.com (ChatGPT Custom Instructions) and aiprm.com.
metadata.one_idea: A prompt is only as good as the context behind it, and the cost of missing context scales with how much the tool is allowed to do. Pepper's distinguishing move is that it shows you what it had to guess instead of inventing it — and the project is to verify, on the live sites, the one link its tests cannot see.
metadata.tts_note: Every figure is written as words. 'Uh-mohg Muddoor' is a phonetic respelling used in narration_text ONLY: the literal spelling 'Maddur' phonemizes to /mˈædjʊɹ/ ('MAD-yoor'), heard back by ASR as 'Madger'. The respelling gives /ˈʌmˈoʊɡ mˈʌdɔːɹ/. Never on screen. 'AIPRM' is never spoken (no letter-by-letter sequences); it appears on screen only.
metadata.voice_note: am_puck — the voice chosen by spectral-centroid measurement for the previous reel (2883 Hz vs am_onyx 1748 Hz) and already round-tripped clean through ASR. Reused because it has no known defects.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — opens on the composer, ask lands answered. Leads with the PROBLEM a user hits in real use, not with test output (testing moved to B06). HONESTY: the composer is a reconstructed UI and NO MODEL WAS RUN — the chip says so. The three lines under it are not a reply; they are labelled 'missing:' annotations of what the request leaves out, read aloud as they appear. Narrated as myself; the voice declares itself synthetic in the first breath.
beats.narration_text: Hello. This is Uh-mohg Muddoor. The voice is synthetic; the claims are mine. You open an AI chat and type: help me write a cover letter. It doesn't know who you are, what the job is, or what to avoid. So it has to guess. Tomorrow you'll type that background again, or set it up separately on every site you use.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — whole idea in one breath, written in front of the viewer. The correction IS the misconception this film dismantles: that getting more from AI is about phrasing. Single-word triggers because the component matches per whitespace token. Both triggers are corrected so no wrong fragment survives: final text reads 'Getting more from AI / is a context problem. / Fix the background, / fix the answer.'
beats.narration_text: Here it is in one breath. Getting more from AI is not a wording problem. It is a context problem. Fix the background, and you fix the answer. And the more a tool is allowed to do, the more the missing background costs.

beats.role_note: Q1 — what it is, as a user meets it. The six slots are the six parts Pepper's panel shows; each lands as its plain-language description is spoken. 'What you've already told it' = the profile questions, answered once and kept in the browser. The footer names the five sites it is BUILT for — not 'works on': it has only been tested on mock pages of them. Implementation detail (lib/core.js) was removed from this beat.
beats.narration_text: Here is what Pepper does about it. You type the same rough request. Pepper turns it into a full prompt, using what you've already told it: who the AI should be, the background it can't guess, what to write, the rules, the layout, and what done looks like. It drops that in the box. You press send.

beats.role_note: The thesis the author set: context matters more the more access an AI has. HONESTY: the bar widths are illustrative, not measured, and the footer says so on screen — the ORDERING is the claim. The stop rung is Pepper's actual boundary (insertIntoSite clicks nothing). The stop rule is drawn BELOW rung 2 — Pepper fills the box and stops before sending. It was first drawn above rung 2, which read as the opposite.
beats.narration_text: Now the argument. Missing context is not one bug with one size. Its cost scales with what the tool may do. A tool that only reads your typing gets you a worse paragraph. A tool that sends for you gets you an answer you never checked. A tool that can act on your account gets you something you cannot undo. Pepper stops at the second rung, on purpose.

beats.role_note: Q2 core — the distinguishing feature, shown on a REAL screenshot: panel-result-model.png, written by Pepper's own browser test (browser.test.js) when I re-ran the suite on this machine on 10 Oct 2026 (Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4, 20/20 checks passing). SHA-256 770d5303…60ad, copied byte-identical; kept in pepper-tests/e2e/shots-2026-10-10/. The package's own 2 Oct copy is unchanged in shots/. It shows the panel on the suite's MOCK ChatGPT page (the page header reads 'ChatGPT (mock)'), rendering the test's MOCKED model reply, with SYNTHETIC fixture data from browser.test.js ('Stripe new-grad SWE role', resume.txt). The caption says all of this on screen. The 'I am applying for roles in the United States.' line is the same example as buildSystemPrompt in lib/core.js. The camera only moves and a ring is drawn outside the image's own UI; no pixel is altered.
beats.narration_text: Here is the part that makes it more than a template. When the prompt needs a fact about you that Pepper does not have, it is not allowed to invent one. Facts may come only from your stored profile, memories and files. Anything else lands in this box, outside the prompt, until you add it yourself. Missing context is shown, not filled.

beats.narration_text: Why not use what already exists? Two of them, read this morning on their own pages. ChatGPT's custom instructions: standing text, applied to every chat, one site, kept on your account. Second, a prompt-library extension with five thousand four hundred templates that somebody else wrote. Both are real, and both are useful. Neither one tells you what it had to guess.

beats.role_note: What exists today, as numbers I can show. BOTH suites were run on this machine on 10 Oct 2026: unit 75/75 (Node v24.13.0, 6.4 s) and browser 20/20 (Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4, 70.3 s; Node reports 22 = two parent groups of 7 and 13 checks). The browser checks run against LOCAL MOCK PAGES and the row label says so. 22 = PNGs in the package's e2e/shots (the package's 26 PNGs include four icons; first drafted as 26 and caught). count:false — a rolling '37 of 75' frame would be a false result on screen. The zero is the damning row. The header names BOTH commands that ran; it first named only the unit-test command, above a browser row it did not produce.
beats.narration_text: So what actually exists. The suite ran this morning, on this machine. Seventy-five unit tests, seventy-five passing, in about six seconds. Twenty browser checks, re-run today, all passing. Twenty-two screenshots that suite produced. And one more number, the one nobody puts in bold: how many live sites any of it has touched.

beats.role_note: Q6 — the one concrete risk and its mitigation. 'best-effort … MUST be re-verified' is verbatim from the comment above SITES in lib/core.js. The 99% threshold is the project's own N4 condition. The 'after' sentence deliberately contains BLANKS, not a number: no result has been measured, so none is shown. The evidence rows are verbatim: SITES[chatgpt].input in lib/core.js and the ChatGPT mock in pepper-tests/e2e/mock-sites.js line 42. The strike covers ONLY 'so insertion works': '75 tests pass' is true — the unsupported part is the inference. It first struck the whole sentence, which would have struck a true claim.
beats.narration_text: Here is what could sink it, and it is not subtle. Every one of those checks ran against mock pages, and the mocks were built from Pepper's own selectors. So the tests cannot catch a wrong selector. They are made of it. The fix is a measurement: twenty inserts per live site, against the project's own bar of ninety-nine percent, re-run every Chrome release.

beats.role_note: Q5 — the one thing it deliberately will not do. Each row is checkable in the package: insertIntoSite dispatches no key events and clicks nothing (content.js); the manifest's permissions are exactly storage + unlimitedStorage; PRIVACY.md 'Pepper never reads the rest of the page'. HONESTY: C17 marks 'never submits' as 'Pass on mocks; code read' with the live row blank — the footer says exactly that.
beats.narration_text: And the one thing it will never do. Pepper will not press send. That is not a missing feature; it is the boundary. It asks for two browser permissions. It reads the prompt box, not the page. The moment a tool sends for you, it needs permission to act, and acting on context nobody checked is where the damage starts.

beats.role_note: What the pitch does not establish — the course's own move pointed at the author's own claim. Each condition is from CHANGES.md: selectors untested live (C17, H7 open), the model was mocked ('Not tested, or known limits'), no user has run it (H5–H8 and H13–H14 open). The claim and question land on their words (claimAt / questionAt); they were hardcoded to 0.04 / 0.20, three seconds ahead of the narration.
beats.narration_text: Now the part a pitch usually skips. Point the same question at my own claim. What would have to be true for 'Pepper works' to be wrong? Three conditions, and not one of them has been tested. The selectors could be stale. A real model might ignore the six-part contract; every model in those tests was a fake. And nobody but me has ever opened it.

beats.role_note: Q7 — why this project, and which half is showing off. AUTHORSHIP, from CHANGES.md: v0.3 was built as 'Claude steps' C1–C17 against my design document; the 'Human steps' H1–H14 are mine and H2–H14 are open. So the left column claims what I did (specify, direct), not code I did not write. Q3 (who opens it, first 60 seconds) is the last sentence: run the tests, then find the column of unsupported claims. Headings shortened to ALREADY DONE / NOT DONE YET: the longer ones wrapped and the heading rule cut them in half.
beats.narration_text: So why this one? Half is showing off, and I will say which. I designed Pepper and directed the build; Claude wrote the code, and the tests went green. The other half is new: running a check that can come back bad, and publishing the number anyway. Anyone opening this repository should run the tests in a minute, then find that column.

beats.role_note: The verdict page carries the brief's two closing lists. It is labelled as PROJECT-BRIEF.md, my document, not as a Claude reply. Lines are bare sentences (the component strips lead numbers).
beats.narration_text: So, the verdict, in two lists. Exists today: the extension, seventy-five passing tests, twenty-two screenshots, a protocol with every result cell blank, and a draft privacy notice. Will exist: that protocol run on five live sites, a measured insert rate for each, a failure analysis, and a check that fails loudly when a site moves its box. Nothing in the second list has happened yet.

Will exist: a failure analysis, and a check that fails loudly when a site moves its box.
It will never press send. That is the boundary, not a gap.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — the prompt is read aloud verbatim, then discussed. No output lines: nothing has been run, so nothing is shown as an answer. The chip says so.
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and here is the prompt. Take the last tool you shipped. List every claim its README makes. Beside each one, write the exact test that supports it, and where there is none, write: nobody has checked this. Then count the second column. That count separates what you know from what you have been saying. Run it on your own repository. The number is usually worse than you expect.
